name: Ignatius of Antioch
knownFor: Bishop of Antioch whose seven letters, written under guard on the way to his death at Rome, warn the churches to keep to their bishops and to Christ who truly suffered.
dates: Bishop of Antioch early in the second century; died under the emperor Trajan in Eusebius of Caesarea's placing, or under Hadrian in Harnack's
place: Antioch in Syria; Smyrna and Troas on the road to Rome

keyWorks.title: Letter to the Romans
keyWorks.about: his plea that the church at Rome not save him from the beasts

keyWorks.title: Letter to the Smyrnaeans
keyWorks.about: against those who said Christ only seemed to suffer, and for doing nothing in the church without the bishop; where the phrase "Catholic Church" first appears, Cleveland Coxe says

keyWorks.title: Letter to Polycarp
keyWorks.about: to the bishop of Smyrna, who in Eusebius's account is asked to care for the flock at Antioch

traces: He told the church at Smyrna that wherever the bishop appears the people should be, "even as, wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the Catholic Church", in the English of A. Roberts and J. Donaldson. Cleveland Coxe, who edited the American edition, notes that this is the first use of the phrase in the early church's writings.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus, in his Dialogues, set the letter to the Smyrnaeans among the testimonies that Christ was "crucified for our sake in the flesh", in Blomfield Jackson's English.
remembered: Polycarp of Smyrna, in his letter to the Philippians, holds up "the blessed Ignatius" as an example of patience, and sends the Philippians the letters of Ignatius he had.
Irenaeus of Lyon quotes the wheat line as the words of "a certain man of ours" condemned to the wild beasts. Eusebius of Caesarea gives Irenaeus's words as "As one of our people said."
Eusebius of Caesarea names all seven letters and says his fame "is still celebrated by a great many."

uncertain: What came of his rule. The sources used here do not show what came of his rule on bishops in other churches, and Eusebius gives his death at Rome only as what "report says".

Arthur McGiffert, who translated Eusebius, says we must turn to the letters for "our chief knowledge of his life". Eusebius adds that he was the second bishop of Antioch after Peter; McGiffert says Origen had already said so, and that it rests on a tradition at least partly independent of the letters.

Which letters are his was argued for a long time. Fifteen carry his name; eight are set aside as forgeries. Daillé, in 1666, rejected the letters in every form then known. Bishop Pearson defended the seven shorter Greek letters in 1672. William Cureton, in 1845, argued that the three letters in a Syriac version were nearest to what Ignatius wrote; Bunsen agreed with him and Hefele did not. McGiffert wrote in 1890 that Zahn and Lightfoot had settled it for the shorter Greek letters, though their genuineness "is still stoutly denied by some".

The date of his death. Eusebius places him in the reign of Trajan, and his Chronicle dates the death to Trajan's tenth year, about 107; McGiffert calls the Chronicle's dates for these bishops of Antioch "entirely unreliable". Zahn and Lightfoot would say only that he died under Trajan. Harnack placed it under Hadrian. Here he is placed only early in the second century, which all of them allow.
Accounts of his martyrdom were written from the fourth century on. McGiffert says they are "quite contradictory" and furnish "no trustworthy information".

The wheat line. Other English forms in the same volume read "I am ground" and "the pure bread of God": the longer form of the letter, and Irenaeus's quotation ("the wheat of Christ ... the pure bread of God"). The words quoted above follow the shorter form, which reads "let me be ground". The Greek is not held here.

briefReferences: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History III.22 and III.36.1-2, tr. Arthur McGiffert: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, in the time Eusebius gives to Trajan, early in the second century.

Ignatius, Letter to the Romans 4-5, tr. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson: a condemned man, writing to Rome not to hinder his death; "bound to ten leopards, I mean a band of soldiers"; the wheat of God ground by the beasts.
Eusebius, Church History III.36.3-6, tr. McGiffert: sent from Syria to Rome for the beasts, through Asia under military guard; from Smyrna to the church of Rome, begging them not to save him.
Eusebius, Church History III.36.5 and 10, tr. McGiffert: the six other letters, to Ephesus, Magnesia and Tralles from Smyrna, and to Philadelphia, Smyrna and Polycarp from Troas.
Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 2 and 4, tr. Roberts and Donaldson: those who said Christ only seemed to suffer; his chains as the answer.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus, Dialogue 1, tr. Blomfield Jackson: the letter to the Smyrnaeans as testimony that Christ was crucified in the flesh.
Ignatius, Letter to the Smyrnaeans 8, tr. Roberts and Donaldson: nothing in the church without the bishop; what he approves is secure and valid.
Polycarp of Smyrna, Letter to the Philippians 13, tr. Roberts and Donaldson: the letters of Ignatius sent to Philippi.
Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies V.28.4, tr. A. Roberts and W. H. Rambaut: the wheat saying as the words of a man of ours condemned to the beasts.
Eusebius, Church History III.36.2-3 and 5-15, tr. McGiffert: his death at Rome as report; the seven letters named; his fame still celebrated by many.
World census, Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity: his tradition.
